records.title: Disease burden attributable to intimate partner violence against females and sexual violence against children in 204 countries and territories, 1990-2023: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
records.design: GBD modelling study (systematic analysis, spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression + burden-of-proof risk methodology)
records.population_setting: 204 countries and territories, females aged 15+ (IPV) and males/females (sexual violence against children), 1990-2023
records.key_finding: In 2023, an estimated 608 million (95% UI 518-724) females aged 15+ had ever been exposed to IPV, contributing 18.5 million (8.74-30.0) DALYs; IPV ranked as the 4th leading risk factor for DALYs among females aged 15-49. Anxiety disorders and major depressive disorder were the leading IPV-attributed health outcomes (5.43 million and 3.96 million DALYs respectively).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly grounds the marriage-transition-as-governance-threshold rationale and the primary-prevention framing of T-PHE by quantifying IPV as a top-tier global disease burden driver; supports the rationale for P1 (decision control as a mechanism worth intervening on) but is a burden-of-disease estimate, not evidence T-PHE itself works.

records.title: Global, regional, and national prevalence estimates of physical or sexual, or both, intimate partner violence against women in 2018.
records.design: Systematic review + Bayesian multilevel modelling of prevalence data
records.population_setting: 366 eligible studies, 2 million women, 161 countries/areas, ever-partnered women aged 15-49
records.key_finding: Globally, 27% (UI 23-31%) of ever-partnered women aged 15-49 have experienced physical or sexual, or both, IPV in their lifetime, with 13% (10-16%) in the past year; violence starts early, affecting 24% (UI 21-28%) of women aged 15-19 and 26% (23-30%) aged 20-24.
records.relevance_to_tphe: WHO/LSHTM global prevalence baseline underlying the burden argument for a marriage-transition governance threshold (P1); shows IPV risk is already established before/around the age most premarital couples marry, supporting the rationale for intervening at the marriage transition rather than proving T-PHE's effectiveness.
records.evidence_level: Systematic review with statistical modelling (global surveillance estimate)

records.title: Findings from the SASA! Study: a cluster randomized controlled trial to assess the impact of a community mobilization intervention to prevent violence against women and reduce HIV risk in Kampala, Uganda.
records.design: Pair-matched cluster randomized controlled trial (8 communities)
records.population_setting: Community members aged 18-49, Kampala, Uganda; baseline n=1,583, follow-up n=2,532
records.key_finding: SASA! was associated with significantly lower social acceptance of IPV among women (aRR 0.54, 95% CI 0.38-0.79) and 52% lower past-year physical IPV among women (0.48, 95% CI 0.16-1.39, crossing 1), plus higher likelihood of women receiving supportive community responses to disclosed violence.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P1/P2 (governance-layer, community-level mechanisms and visibility of concerns can shift norms and responses) but the physical-IPV effect's wide confidence interval crossing 1 is a caution relevant to T-PHE's own FAILURE CRITERION discipline about not over-claiming from attitudinal/knowledge shifts alone.

records.title: Ecological pathways to prevention: How does the SASA! community mobilisation model work to prevent physical intimate partner violence against women?
records.first_author: Michau L / Kyegombe N (secondary mediation analysis of SASA! CRT)
records.design: Secondary mediation analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial
records.population_setting: Community members aged 18-49, Kampala, Uganda (SASA! trial communities)
records.key_finding: Community-level normative attitudes were the most important mediators of SASA!'s effect on physical IPV, explaining 70% of the effect on women's experience of IPV and 95% of the effect on men's perpetration; men's reduced suspicion of partner infidelity explained 22% of the effect on perpetration.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Programme-theory/logic-model evidence that norms-change (not knowledge/attendance alone) is the operative mechanism for reducing IPV, directly supporting T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION logic that knowledge/attendance/satisfaction rising without deeper mechanism change (informed choice, coercion recognition) would not constitute success.
records.evidence_level: Mediation analysis nested in a cluster RCT

records.title: Cost and cost-effectiveness analysis of a community mobilisation intervention to reduce intimate partner violence in Kampala, Uganda.
records.design: Economic evaluation alongside a cluster randomized controlled trial
records.population_setting: SASA! intervention communities, Kampala, Uganda, provider perspective, 4 years of programming
records.key_finding: Total intervention cost over 4 years was estimated at US$553,252, averaging US$5 per person reached annually; an estimated 1,201 cases of past-year physical IPV were averted (90% CI 97-2,307) at a cost of US$460 per case averted.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant background for resourcing referral and safeguard infrastructure (P5, bounded authority and referral) in a conceptual synthesis that must reckon with feasibility of implementing multi-component safeguards, though it is a cost analysis of a different (community mobilization) programme model, not premarital education.
records.evidence_level: Economic evaluation nested in a cluster RCT

records.title: SASA! Together: An evolution of the SASA! approach to prevent violence against women.
records.design: Programme-theory/programme-description paper (non-empirical evaluation article)
records.population_setting: Raising Voices programme learning, Uganda-originated model adapted for broader use
records.key_finding: The paper describes the rationale for revising SASA! after ten years of programme learning and research, detailing how the revised 'SASA! Together' model incorporated field learning, and reflects on debates such as how best to scale up violence-prevention programmes.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports P7 (repairability) as a real-world precedent: an evidence-informed IPV-prevention programme explicitly built a formal revision cycle from accumulated field learning rather than treating its original design as fixed.

records.title: Exploring Couples' Processes of Change in the Context of SASA!, a Violence Against Women and HIV Prevention Intervention in Uganda.
records.design: Qualitative dyadic study (in-depth interviews, framework analysis)
records.population_setting: Couples in SASA! intervention communities, Kampala, Uganda
records.key_finding: Engagement with SASA! activities and relationship-skills/communication learning was associated with reduced conflict and IPV for many couples and increased trust, respect and joint economic problem-solving, though experiences and degree of change varied widely across couples.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Illustrates a plausible mechanism for P1 (relationship-skills/communication content strengthening decision control and reducing conflict) but is drawn from ongoing established couples in a community-mobilisation context, not premarital screening; it does not test or validate T-PHE's STOP RULE logic that joint work must halt where coercive control is suspected, since this cohort was not selected for known violence risk.

records.title: Effective prevention of intimate partner violence through couples training: a randomised controlled trial of Indashyikirwa in Rwanda.
records.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial (28 sectors)
records.population_setting: Couples recruited from village savings and loan associations, rural Rwanda; 828 women/821 men intervention, 832 women/830 men control
records.key_finding: At 24 months, women in intervention sectors were less likely to report physical/sexual IPV (aRR 0.44, 95% CI 0.34-0.59) and men less likely to report perpetration (aRR 0.54, 95% CI 0.38-0.75), with additional gains in acceptability of wife-beating, conflict management, communication, trust and self-efficacy, and no study-related harms detected.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Strong supporting precedent for a structured couples-curriculum approach analogous to T-PHE: a couples-based curriculum plus community safeguards achieved a large, statistically robust reduction in IPV; the explicit 'no study-related harms' finding is relevant evidence that couples training, when structured, need not itself increase risk, but this trial screened via VSLA membership rather than a formal STOP RULE for suspected coercive control.

records.title: Shifting and transforming gender-inequitable beliefs, behaviours and norms in intimate partnerships: the Indashyikirwa couples' programme in Rwanda.
records.design: Longitudinal qualitative study
records.population_setting: Heterosexual couples participating in the Indashyikirwa curriculum, Rwanda
records.key_finding: The curriculum, designed to build relationship skills and reduce gender-inequitable beliefs/behaviours/norms underpinning IPV, was associated with reported shifts in individual beliefs, couple relationship dynamics and gender norms among participating couples over time.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Qualitative mechanism evidence supporting P1 (a structured relationship-skills curriculum can plausibly strengthen the individual/couple-level decision-control processes T-PHE targets), complementary to the Indashyikirwa RCT (PMID 33355268).

records.title: Lessons learned from implementing Indashyikirwa in Rwanda - an adaptation of the SASA! approach to prevent and respond to intimate partner violence.
records.design: Implementation/adaptation review (qualitative evaluation and programme documentation)
records.population_setting: Indashyikirwa programme, implemented by CARE Rwanda, RWAMREC and RWN, rural Rwanda
records.key_finding: Indashyikirwa combined a 5-month couples curriculum, sustained community activism by trained couples, women's safe spaces for dedicated support and referral of IPV survivors, and training of opinion leaders to support an enabling environment; adaptation was guided by the SASA! fidelity brief.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Close structural precedent for T-PHE's own multi-component safeguard architecture: it pairs a couples curriculum with a dedicated confidential referral pathway (women's safe spaces) and a defined enabling/authority structure, paralleling P4 (stop rule pending assessment), P5 (bounded authority and referral) and the affected-person-visibility safeguard.

records.title: Shifting Norms in Faith Communities to Reduce Intimate Partner Violence: Results from a Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial of the Masculinity, Faith, and Peace Program in Nigeria.
records.design: Two-arm, mixed-methods cluster randomized controlled trial (18-month faith-based, norms-shifting programme)
records.population_setting: Women aged 18-35 (n=350) and male partners (n=281), from 10 Muslim and 10 Christian congregations, Plateau State, Nigeria
records.key_finding: The Masculinity, Faith, and Peace (MFP) programme, delivered through faith congregations, assessed shifts in individual-, couple- and community-level social norms and IPV incidence in a mixed Muslim/Christian congregational sample; the trial was explicitly designed and powered to evaluate norms-shifting mechanisms rather than knowledge/attendance alone.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly relevant to P3 (cultural/religious tailoring, tested here across parallel Muslim and Christian congregations in one rigorous trial) and to the feasibility of delivering faith-based IPV-prevention content through religious leadership structures resembling T-PHE's premarital setting.

records.title: Korean clergy for healthy families: online intervention for preventing intimate partner violence.
records.design: Randomized controlled pilot trial (online modules, baseline and 3-month follow-up)
records.population_setting: Korean American faith leaders, southeastern USA (n=55; intervention n=27, control n=28)
records.key_finding: The intervention group showed significant improvement in knowledge of IPV resources and attitudes against IPV compared to control, but gains in self-efficacy and prevention/intervention behaviours, while greater than control, were not statistically significant.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly relevant to P5 (referral quality) since clergy are a plausible bounded-authority referral node, but the null result for self-efficacy/behaviour change is a cautionary complication for T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION: raising knowledge/attitudes among gatekeepers does not guarantee improved safe help-seeking or accountable referral behaviour.

records.title: Qualitative Assessment of Key Implementation Factors in a Faith-Based Response to Intimate Partner Violence.
records.first_author: Le V (Archdiocese of Chicago Domestic Violence Outreach study)
records.design: Qualitative implementation study (16 semi-structured interviews, CFIR-coded)
records.population_setting: Catholic diocesan and parish leadership, Archdiocese of Chicago Domestic Violence Outreach, USA
records.key_finding: Using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, seven inner-setting constructs (leadership structure, culture, resources, networking/communication, access to knowledge, compatibility with parish values, leadership engagement) were identified as facilitators of successful diocesan-level IPV response implementation.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P5 (accountable referral requires organizational structure, not just goodwill) by showing that a faith institution's capacity to run an IPV response programme depends on defined leadership, resourcing and networked communication, structural preconditions T-PHE's bounded-authority safeguard would also need in a religious-organisation delivery setting.

records.title: Pathways of change: qualitative evaluations of intimate partner violence prevention programmes in Ghana, Rwanda, South Africa and Tajikistan.
records.design: Comparative qualitative case study (secondary thematic analysis)
records.population_setting: Participants across four IPV-prevention programmes, What Works to Prevent Violence against Women and Girls Programme (Ghana, Rwanda, South Africa, Tajikistan)
records.key_finding: Similar cross-context pathways of change were identified: learning and applying relationship skills, participatory challenge of harmful gender norms with group rapport, and integration of economic-empowerment activities to reduce drivers of IPV and build self-confidence.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Cross-context programme-theory evidence supporting P1 (relationship-skills content as a plausible mechanism for decision control) and P3 (participatory, culturally embedded delivery matters for whether norms-challenging content is accepted), useful for grounding T-PHE's programme theory in convergent findings across diverse settings rather than a single trial.

records.title: Equipping community health workers in Rwanda to deliver a gender transformative parenting program to prevent violence.
records.design: Pre/post training evaluation with phone follow-up
records.population_setting: 573 community health workers, Burera district, Rwanda, delivering the Bandebereho programme at scale
records.key_finding: Of 562 CHWs completing the pre-survey and 564 the post-survey (6-9 months later, plus 506 at 17-19 month follow-up), CHWs showed more equitable gender attitudes post-training; facilitators with more education showed smaller attitude shifts, underscoring the importance of sufficient time for facilitators' own transformation to maintain fidelity at scale.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to bounded-authority/facilitator-competence safeguards: shows that scaling a violence-prevention curriculum through non-specialist community delivery agents (analogous to premarital course facilitators) requires structured, adequately dosed training to preserve fidelity, a caution for any scale-up of a T-PHE-style programme.

records.title: Effectiveness of the Moments that Matter parenting programme on caregiving practices, family violence, mental health and other outcomes: a cluster-randomised controlled trial in Kenya.
records.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial
records.population_setting: 595 caregiver-child dyads (children aged 0-18 months) in 46 villages, western Kenya, delivered via community volunteers partnered with faith leaders
records.key_finding: At endline there were no overall intervention effects on the primary outcome (child development), though moderate-to-large effects were observed on several secondary outcomes including caregiver stimulation, harsh discipline, caregiver mental health, social support, and intimate partner violence victimisation as reported by female caregivers.
records.relevance_to_tphe: A directly cautionary case for T-PHE's FAILURE CRITERION: a rigorously trialled, faith-leader-partnered community programme showed a null result on its declared primary outcome while showing improvement on secondary/downstream outcomes (including IPV victimisation), illustrating exactly the kind of outcome-selection pitfall T-PHE's failure criterion is designed to guard against (do not let secondary or proxy gains substitute for the declared primary target).

records.title: Community based intervention to prevent domestic violence against women in the reproductive age in Northwestern Ethiopia: a study protocol for community based cluster randomized trial.
records.design: Study protocol for a community-based quasi-experimental/cluster trial
records.population_setting: 1,269 women planned across intervention, active comparator and control groups, Awi zone, northwestern Ethiopia
records.key_finding: The protocol describes a planned pilot of translating existing evidence and policy into community-level domestic-violence prevention via peer education, community representative training, husband involvement and integration with community health extension programmes; no outcome data are reported (protocol only).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Illustrates the broader field's emphasis on husband/partner involvement and community health-worker integration as delivery channels for IPV prevention (echoing P1's governance-layer logic), but as a protocol paper it provides no outcome evidence and should not be cited for effectiveness.

records.title: Community activism as a strategy to reduce intimate partner violence (IPV) in rural Rwanda: Results of a community randomised trial.
records.design: Cluster randomized controlled trial (community-level activism component)
records.population_setting: Rural Rwanda, adaptation of the SASA! community-activism model
records.key_finding: There was no evidence of an intervention effect on any primary or secondary trial outcome, including women's past-year experience of physical and/or sexual IPV from a current partner (adjusted odds ratio 1.25, 95% CI 0.92-1.70), i.e. a null/non-significant result in the direction of possible harm.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly complicates any assumption that community-mobilisation or norms-based prevention strategies reliably reduce IPV: a rigorous RCT of an adapted, well-regarded model found no protective effect, reinforcing the need for T-PHE's own FAILURE CRITERION and epistemic-humility safeguard rather than assuming a plausible-sounding mechanism will translate into real protection.

records.title: Changing the norms that drive intimate partner violence: findings from a cluster randomised trial on what predisposes bystanders to intervene.
records.design: Cross-sectional survey nested within a cluster randomised trial (SASA! study)
records.population_setting: Community members aged 18-49 who had witnessed IPV, Kampala, Uganda, 4 years post-intervention
records.key_finding: SASA! community members who had witnessed IPV were substantially more likely to try to help than control-community counterparts (57% vs 31%); associated factors differed by trial arm, with SASA!-community bystander action linked to relationship duration, employment, talking to neighbours and SASA! exposure.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P2 (a norms-shifted community/social environment increases visibility of, and willingness to respond to, concerns about violence), relevant background for why T-PHE frames private-channel and community-facing safeguards as complementary rather than substitutable.
records.evidence_level: Cross-sectional survey nested in a cluster RCT

records.title: Adapting, Sustaining and Scaling Violence against Women and Children Prevention Interventions in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Scoping Review of Implementation Science Approaches.
records.design: Scoping review
records.population_setting: 40 VAW/C evaluation studies with implementation or process-evaluation components (2023-2024 review period), low- and middle-income country focus
records.key_finding: Commonly used implementation frameworks were CFIR, EPIS and MRC frameworks, with fidelity, acceptability and feasibility most studied; scale and sustainability, and survivor-centred practice/practice-based knowledge, were only minimally addressed in the reviewed literature.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly relevant to T-PHE's status as a programme-theory/logic-model synthesis: confirms that formal implementation-science framing (which T-PHE's six safeguards and stop rule resemble) is under-used in VAW/C prevention research and that scale/sustainability and survivor-centredness remain evidence gaps, supporting T-PHE's own epistemic-humility framing rather than a claim of proven effectiveness.

gaps_noted: No PubMed-indexed paper was found that evaluates a premarital or pre-nuptial education programme specifically structured around a governance/decision-control framework comparable to T-PHE; the closest analogues (SASA!, Indashyikirwa, MFP) are ongoing-couple or community-level interventions, not marriage-transition-timed interventions.

No paper directly evaluates a formal 'stop rule' halting joint couple education pending confidential risk assessment where coercive control is suspected; Indashyikirwa's women's safe spaces (PMID 30125773) are the closest structural analogue but are not framed as a stop/pause mechanism tied to joint sessions.

The WHO RESPECT women framework's own core normative document (WHO/UN Women/UNFPA 2019, and its 2nd edition) is guidance, not a PubMed-indexed primary study, and could not be retrieved via esearch/efetch under this search's PubMed-only constraint; it should be cited separately via its official WHO URL/ISBN per the angle brief rather than via a PMID.

No papers were found specifically evaluating IPV-prevention programme mechanisms among Muslim or intercultural couples in Thailand or Southeast Asia; the Nigerian Muslim/Christian congregational trial (PMID 37329160) is the nearest cross-cultural, mixed-faith analogue found.

Faith-based intervention evidence located skews toward Christian/Catholic and one Korean-immigrant Christian clergy sample plus one Nigerian Muslim/Christian trial; specifically Islamic religious-authority-led premarital education evaluations were not located in this search.

Cost-effectiveness and implementation-science evidence located pertains to community mobilisation and CHW-delivered parenting/couples programmes, not premarital education delivered through religious institutions, limiting direct transferability to T-PHE's delivery channel.
limits_of_this_search: This search used 12 PubMed E-utilities queries (6 initial plus 6 targeted follow-ups) restricted to PubMed-indexed literature; 20 of the most relevant retrieved records (of ~90 unique PMIDs surfaced across queries) were efetched in full and had their abstracts read before inclusion. Selection was relevance-driven and non-exhaustive (a full systematic review was out of scope); WHO/global guidance documents that are not PubMed-indexed (e.g., the WHO RESPECT women framework itself) were not retrievable through this tool chain and are noted as a gap rather than fabricated with a placeholder PMID. All key findings are drawn from the efetched Article/Abstract XML, not from esummary titles alone.
